title: Why does a crater lake turn cloudy?
bodyMd:
A small crater lake sometimes becomes cloudy after strong winds. The cloudiness consists of mineral particles; samples contain no increase in living algal cells. A lake-bottom spring releases clear water. New cloudy episodes have begun both during daylight and at night; during the nighttime onsets, measured water temperatures remained below the threshold proposed by Investigator3. Three investigators propose explanations. Each model is intended as the sole cause of the mineral cloudiness, not as an additional minor process.

Investigator1: Wind stirs shallow bottom sediment into suspension. Any strong wind can cause cloudiness if it lasts long enough. Spring discharge is not required. If bottom sediment is isolated beneath a particle-tight cover, wind alone should not make the water above that cover cloudy.

Investigator2: Strong wind increases discharge from the bottom spring. The spring water contains dissolved mineral that forms solid particles when mixed with lake water. Loose bottom sediment is not required. If spring flow is diverted away from the lake, strong wind should no longer produce cloudiness. The proposed mineral precipitation does not require light.

Investigator3: Wind only happens to coincide with daytime warming. Mineral particles form when sunlight warms the water above a threshold temperature. Neither loose sediment nor spring discharge is required. Water kept below the threshold should remain clear even during strong winds; water heated above the threshold should become cloudy without wind.

Investigators can use identical tanks of clear lake water, add the same bottom material, direct equal spring-water flow into tanks, stir to imitate wind, control temperature and light, and count suspended mineral particles. Changing a single candidate cause while holding other relevant conditions fixed can distinguish the models.
